contexts: Particularly, PCA is applied to features z ∈ R d from the network backbone, in order to explore the intrinsic structures.
PCA seeks orthogonal directions, i.e., principal components capturing the highest projection variance, so as to keep maximal data information.

PCA can explore the intrinsic patterns residing in low-dimension subspaces spanned by those principal components, and has been studied for learning with modern DNNs, e.g., training algorithms (Li et al., 2023b) and anomaly detection applications (Fang et al., 2024).
The PCA reconstruction error quantitatively measures the captured information along projection directions.

• A new MU method named LOFT is proposed by leveraging PCA-based subspace learning, simply doing one-shot feature fetching and updating a projection matrix as a plugged-in module into the pretrained model.

This correspondingly leads to the optimization problem for the projection directions capturing maximal information: the sub-space spanned by the eigenvectors of M with the m largest eigenvalues is obtained by solving min U ∈ St( l,m ) Tr( M − UU ⊤ MUU ⊤ ) , which also corresponds to the reconstruction error of PCA as similarly explained in Sec 4.1 of (Avron et al., 2014).

Proposition 4.1 (Pandey et al., 2022) formalizes the optimization problem for obtaining the projection directions capturing minimal information in PCA with Stiefel manifold, where M denotes the covariance matrix.
PCA has long been a fundamental tool in machine learning and beyond (Pearson, 1901).
With the spirits from PCA, we design a novel objective to optimize a projection matrix applied to the feature covariances, such that in the projected subspace the features w.r.t.
In this work, we follow the spirits of PCA for MU by learning the projection directions associated with the low-dimensional feature subspace from f pre .

Towards the feature separability for unlearning, LOFT follows the spirits from PCA to seek such a subspace (to optimize U ), in which the information of Z prerm is maximally captured and meanwhile that of the forgetting features Z gets minimally described.

Note that once the features are fetched, calculations to the covariance matrix are one-shot, since our PCA-based optimization does not vary the covariance matrix, but only updates projection directions for learning the feature subspace that well distinguishes the knowledge between D rm and D fg .
Accordingly, we propose LOFT through PCA-based techniques to learn a projection matrix, thereby constructing a feature subspace that preserves the knowledge of D rm and diminishes that of D fg .
We apply PCA to the remaining features Z rm and obtain U rm ∈ R d × s projecting features onto the s -dimensional subspace.

This optimization is implemented following the spirits of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) (Pearson, 1901): A projection matrix is trained and inserted into the pretrained model, requiring only two feature covariance matrices of D fg and D rm .
